itinerary.cal: No advance permit reservation needed for this zone — self-register a wilderness permit at the Marblemount Wilderness Info Center; best conditions are typically late July through September once Terror Creek and the approach gullies have melted out.

days.note: From the Goodell Creek Trailhead (600 ft), follow the old road bed then the Terror Creek climber's path — a notoriously brushy, hard-to-follow route with a creek crossing — up to a bench camp around 6,000 ft. This is widely considered one of the harder approaches in the Cascades; expect route-finding and heavy brush even in good conditions.
days.title: Approach to Terror Basin / Stump Hollow
days.objective: Reach the 6,000 ft basin below the Southern Pickets

days.note: Cross the Barrier and traverse into Crescent Creek Basin (~5,800 ft), staying high along the bushy ridge. Short mileage but slow, exposed sidehill travel; many parties treat this as a half-day and use the rest to scout the route or rest before the summit push.
days.title: Move to Crescent Creek Basin
days.objective: Position camp below the peak's south/east side

days.note: A long alpine day: cross the Otto-Himmel col and traverse below the Twin Spires and the Rake to reach the base of the North Face, then climb the sustained buttress (5.8, much of it simul-climbed) to the 8,151 ft summit before reversing the route or dropping to the south side to get back to camp.
days.title: North Face / Stoddard-North Buttress summit push

schedule.label: Leave Crescent Creek Basin camp
schedule.detail: Alpine start with headlamps toward the Otto-Himmel col.

schedule.label: Cross the col, traverse to the north side
schedule.detail: Even fast parties need 2-3 hr from Crescent Creek Basin to reach the base of the north face.

schedule.label: Rope up at the base of the North Face
schedule.detail: Start of the 2,500 ft Stoddard/North Buttress line, 5.8.

schedule.label: Top out on the summit
schedule.detail: 8,151 ft; a long, sustained buttress climb.

schedule.label: Begin the descent
schedule.detail: Rappel/downclimb the route, or drop to the south side toward camp.

schedule.label: Back at Crescent Creek Basin camp
schedule.detail: A 15+ hr day; build in a weather/rest buffer if possible.

days.objective: Climb the 2,500 ft North Face and return to camp

days.note: Reverse the approach: back over the Barrier, down through Terror Basin, and out the Terror Creek climber's path to the trailhead. Brush is easier to push through downhill but navigation errors are still common.
days.title: Hike out
days.objective: Return to the Goodell Creek Trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A 4-day trip: two hard bushwhack approach days to Crescent Creek Basin, one very long (14-15 hr) technical day on the 2,500 ft North Face/Stoddard-North Buttress line, and a day to hike out.

climbing_route.label: Glacier crossing and start of the face
climbing_route.notes: The wall is accessed from its west side after crossing the glacier remnant beneath it, and the start is just left of the snowfield at the bottom of the face. Third and fourth class scrambling on comparatively solid rock leads up to and above that snowpatch. The ice below is small but broken and mostly unbridged by mid-season, so it is treated as glacier travel; the moat where snow meets rock at the base is the usual obstacle.

climbing_route.label: Lower face rising traverse
climbing_route.notes: Long, mostly third class pitches climb above the snowfield while traversing steadily rightward. The route takes the right, or western, of the two ribs that split the north face. Parties simul-climb much of this. The main risk here is not difficulty but committing to the wrong rib — the line is defined by where you exit at the top, and the face is over 2,000 ft tall with limited options to reverse.

climbing_route.label: Dihedrals to the buttress crest
climbing_route.notes: The ascending traverse steepens and follows dihedrals and cracks, aiming for the right or western crest of the buttress about two thirds of the way up the lower face, identifiable by the rock darkening. A sharp prow marks roughly the lower third of the buttress. Time on the crest itself is brief and reported as no harder than 5.7 on generally clean, solid rock.

climbing_route.label: Chimney back on the face
climbing_route.notes: Move back left off the crest onto the face and aim for a chimney above an awkward belay. Reported difficulty here varies with the exact line: some parties keep it to about 5.4, while a variation that traverses further right lower down and takes the true buttress hits a 5.8 traverse crux near the top of the chimney. Upper pitches on this part of the wall have been described as 5.7 to 5.8 on good rock, with the route as a whole graded around III-IV, 5.8.

climbing_route.label: Snow finger, exposed crest and the summits
climbing_route.notes: The long snow finger on the upper face forms a ramp that carries the route for a good distance; carry what you need to climb it. Above its top, the climbing turns to scrambling on a wildly exposed ridge crest, then a traverse around a small tower to the notch between the false and true summits. The false summit is taken directly on an exposed easy fifth class hand traverse, then downclimbed before the short climb to the true 8,151 ft top. Rock quality deteriorates near the top, with steep, extremely loose ground reported; a fatal-consequence rockfall accident on this buttress involved a sizeable block that had appeared solid tearing loose. Descent is normally the West Ridge gully. This is one of the longest and most committing lines in the range and retreat from high on it is genuinely difficult.

before.approach: From the Goodell Creek Group Camp trailhead (elev. ~600 ft, reached via the unpaved Goodell Creek Road that turns north off Highway 20 directly across from Newhalem Campground), follow the old abandoned roadbed/boot path northeast along Goodell Creek for roughly 4 to 4.5 miles — gentle grade, easy walking — to a stone-cairn/arrow junction near 1,700 ft marking the start of the climbers' path up toward Terror Basin. Do not continue straight past the cairn; that fainter track follows Terror Creek toward Crescent Creek Basin and is a separate (and notoriously brushier) approach. Instead take the hard right and start up the steep, well-beaten Terror Basin boot path, which climbs directly and relentlessly through old-growth forest — roughly 3,000+ ft of gain in about 1.5 miles — before breaking out above treeline around 5,000–5,200 ft. Above the trees, a rising traverse across heather benches, slabs, and (early-season) snowfields leads to a broad saddle near 6,200 ft; the standard high camp is in a gravelly, wildflower basin about 400 ft below and beyond the saddle, around 5,700 ft, fed by several small streams (reliable water). From this Terror Basin camp, the North Face/North Ridge is reached by ascending slabs and snow to the saddle between Mount Terror and Mount Degenhardt, then following the short, steep ridge crest directly to the summit. Hazards: the boot path itself is the crux of the approach — steep, root-and-dirt, unrelentingly brushy in places, and physically punishing (widely regarded as one of the harder approaches in the Pickets); expect loose rock and route-finding on the upper slabs approaching the saddle; if the alternate Terror Creek/Crescent Creek Basin line is used, a creek ford or logjam crossing of Terror Creek is required. Most parties treat this as a two-day approach with a high camp rather than a car-to-base push. The technical North Face/Stoddard Buttress start is reached via a traverse from Terror Basin over the Chopping Block col through McMillan Cirque — a steep, brushy descent past slabs and heather beneath Inspiration Peak and the McMillan Spires before rounding into position under Terror's wall. By mid-to-late summer the Terror Glacier remnant at the base is heavily crevassed with mostly unbridged, broken ice; carry glacier travel gear even though it's a small glacier.

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek and the Terror Basin boot path, then over the Chopping Block col through McMillan Cirque to the foot of the wall
approach_variants.notes:
From the Goodell Creek Group Camp trailhead at about 600 ft, reached via the unpaved Goodell Creek Road that turns north off Highway 20 directly across from Newhalem Campground, follow the old abandoned roadbed and boot path northeast along Goodell Creek for roughly 4-4.5 miles of gentle grade to a stone-cairn and arrow junction near 1,700 ft.

DO NOT CONTINUE STRAIGHT PAST THE CAIRN. That fainter track follows Terror Creek toward Crescent Creek Basin and is a separate, notoriously brushier approach. Instead take the HARD RIGHT and start up the steep, well-beaten Terror Basin boot path, which climbs directly through old-growth forest, roughly 3,000-plus ft of gain in about 1.5 miles, before breaking out above treeline around 5,000-5,200 ft.

Above the trees a rising traverse across heather benches, slabs and early-season snowfields leads to a broad saddle near 6,200 ft; the standard high camp is in a gravelly, wildflower basin about 400 ft below and beyond the saddle, around 5,700 ft, fed by several small streams.
hazards: Committing to the wrong rib on a 2,000 ft face with limited options to reverse
A heavily crevassed, mostly unbridged Terror Glacier remnant at the base by mid-season
Steep, extremely loose rock near the top; a fatal-consequence rockfall accident on this buttress involved a block that had appeared solid
A narrow, rockfall-prone descent gully with an undercut melted-out moat by mid to late season
Stuck ropes in the confined descent gully, and a loose, marginal final 100 ft
Retreat from high on the route is genuinely difficult
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START IS JUST LEFT OF THE SNOWFIELD AT THE BOTTOM OF THE FACE, AFTER THE WALL IS ACCESSED FROM ITS WEST SIDE. From Terror Basin the technical start is reached by traversing over the Chopping Block col through McMillan Cirque, a steep, brushy descent past slabs and heather beneath Inspiration Peak and the McMillan Spires, before rounding into position under Terror's wall. Cross the glacier remnant beneath the face, then start JUST LEFT OF THE SNOWPATCH at the bottom.

THE MOAT WHERE SNOW MEETS ROCK AT THE BASE IS THE USUAL OBSTACLE, AND IT IS ALSO THE MARKER: you are at the base when you are standing at the gap between the snowpatch and the wall, on its left.

THE DECISION THAT DEFINES THIS ROUTE, AND IT IS MADE BEFORE THE HARD CLIMBING RATHER THAN DURING IT: THE FACE IS SPLIT BY TWO RIBS, AND THIS ROUTE TAKES THE RIGHT, OR WESTERN, ONE. The main risk on the lower face is not difficulty but committing to the wrong rib. Long, mostly third-class pitches climb above the snowfield while TRAVERSING STEADILY RIGHTWARD; the face is over 2,000 ft tall with limited options to reverse. If your traverse is taking you left, you are on the wrong half of the wall.

TWO CONFIRMATIONS HIGHER, BOTH VISUAL AND BOTH USABLE IN THIN CLOUD: aim for the right or western crest of the buttress about TWO THIRDS OF THE WAY UP THE LOWER FACE, IDENTIFIABLE BY THE ROCK DARKENING. And A SHARP PROW marks roughly the lower third of the buttress. Darkening rock and a sharp prow are features of this rib and not of its neighbour.

WHAT THE UPPER FACE GIVES YOU: a LONG SNOW FINGER forming a ramp that carries the route a good distance, then scrambling on a wildly exposed crest, a traverse around a small tower to the notch between the false and true summits, an exposed easy-fifth hand traverse over the false summit, a downclimb, and the short climb to the true 8,151 ft top.

On the descent, and worth memorising before you leave camp: DO NOT RAPPEL INTO THE LOW NOTCH NORTH OF THE CHOPPING BLOCK. The correct line into Crescent Creek Basin is ABOUT 100 YARDS NORTH OF THAT NOTCH, AT A FLAT, BIVY-SITE SHELF ON THE RIDGE.

before.descent: Rappel and downclimb the route or descend the southern side
before.descent_text: The North Face and any north-side buttress lines are steep and complex enough that essentially no one reverses them — virtually all parties, regardless of which route they climbed, descend via the West Ridge. From the summit, downclimb/scramble the West Ridge crest westward toward the notch between Terror's true and false summits, where a large chockstone marks the top of the descent gully system. From there, work down a narrow, loose, rockfall-prone gully back into Crescent Creek Basin. The exact count varies with snow coverage and route-finding — figure roughly 3–5 rappels total: commonly one or two shorter raps off slung horns/chockstones or fixed pitons-and-a-nut near the ridge crest, followed by two or three more rappels down the gully itself with down-climbing in between. A single 50–60m rope is sufficient for every station reported; anchors are a mix of pre-existing fixed slings/rap rings and natural chockstone/horn anchors that may need backing up with your own gear. Do not rappel into the low notch north of the sub-peak known as the Chopping Block — the correct line into Crescent Creek Basin is about 100 yards north of that notch, at a flat, bivy-site shelf on the ridge. The gully is narrow with little shelter from rockfall, frequently has an undercut, melted-out snow moat by mid-to-late season, and the final ~100 ft is loose and marginal — expect stuck ropes in the confined terrain and manage rope ends carefully. Once down in Crescent Creek Basin, parties either regain the Barrier saddle to return to a Terror Basin camp, or exit directly via the Crescent Creek Basin/Terror Creek climbers' path, which follows the Barrier crest south before dropping to rejoin the Goodell Creek Trail for the hike out.
gear: Glacier travel gear (axe, crampons, thin rope) for the Terror Glacier remnant
Bivy/carry-over gear for a multi-day approach
hazards: Heavily crevassed Terror Glacier remnant with mostly unbridged ice by late summer
Extreme remoteness — a multi-day, off-trail carry-over just to reach the base
Loose rock in the approach gullies and on both the Cooper line and Stoddard Buttress
Complex descent, typically down the opposite (south) side of the mountain
No cell coverage; among the most rescue-difficult terrain in North Cascades NP
before.detailed_rack: A standard alpine rock rack (cams and stoppers to ~3in, several slings/draws) covers the technical ground; add ice axe, crampons, and glacier travel gear (rope, pickets/screws as conditions dictate) for the Ottohorn-Himmel col and Mustard/Terror Glacier crossing.
before.rope_note: Approach via Degenhardt Glacier requiring ice axe/crampons. Lower face ascending traverse mostly 3rd class stepping to 5.7 near the buttress crest; upper face has a long offwidth crack below the false summit.
rack: Cams and stoppers to 3in (medium sizes for the offwidth section)
Ice axe, crampons, thin glacier rope for the Degenhardt/Terror Glacier approach
before.best_season: Late July through August — enough of the season's snow has melted off the approach slabs and gullies for safe travel, while the Terror Glacier remnant is usually still crossable before crevasses open up too much later in the season. Earlier July trips can find firmer snow bridges but far more bugs and brush.

weather.typical: North Cascades alpine weather typical of the range: can shift quickly from clear to socked-in/rain even in summer; north aspect retains snow/ice later into the season

seasonal_hazards.exposure: High consequence - loose protection and loose rock, combined with extreme remoteness, mean a fall or rockfall injury is a serious self-rescue/evacuation problem; wrong-summit route-finding errors on complex ridgelines add to exposure risk

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer route (avalanche forecasting does not cover this remote Southern Pickets objective during its Jul-Sep climbing season)

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: Approach through the Crescent Creek/McMillan Cirque basins may involve glacier/permanent snowfield crossings depending on route to high camp; treat as glaciated approach terrain and rope up where warranted

before.overview: Mount Terror is the highest peak of the savage Southern Pickets. Its north side is the serious side: a 2,500-foot wall of rock, snow, and broken glacier ice dropping into McMillan Cirque, one of the most remote and rarely-visited big walls in the North Cascades. By contrast the south side rises only about 1,000 feet from Crescent Creek Basin. This route line covers Terror's original north-side ascent line; a separate, harder and more sustained buttress (the Stoddard Buttress, 5.8) climbs the same wall further along the crest.

access.fees: $10 per person plus a $6 reservation fee for advance Recreation.gov bookings (youth 15 and under free); walk-up permits at the WIC are free.
access.rules: Bear canisters required or strongly recommended in this zone (available to borrow at the WIC); pack out all waste; group size limits apply in cross-country zones.
access.permit: Free wilderness/climbing permit required for any overnight stay in the park backcountry. As of the 2025–26 permit system, advance reservations are booked on Recreation.gov (a mandatory safety video must be completed, then email noca_wilderness@nps.gov within 3 days of the trip); walk-up permits are otherwise picked up in person at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount, which covers the Terror Basin/McMillan Cirque cross-country zones.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek Group Camp Trailhead
waypoints.note: Off SR-20 near Newhalem; park at Upper Goodell Creek Group Camp and pick up the old roadbed/climbers' path paralleling Goodell Creek — North Cascades NP wilderness permit required for overnight camping.
waypoints.directions: Turn north off Highway 20 directly across from Newhalem Campground onto the unpaved Goodell Creek Road and follow it to the Upper Goodell Creek Group Camp trailhead, at about 600 feet. Park at the group camp and pick up the old roadbed and climbers' path paralleling Goodell Creek. A North Cascades National Park wilderness permit is required for overnight camping; self-register at the Marblemount Wilderness Info Center, and no advance reservation is needed for this zone.

waypoints.name: Terror Creek cairned crossing
waypoints.note: Cairn on the old roadbed marks the log crossing of Terror Creek and the unmarked turnoff onto the Terror Basin climbers' path; a small campsite sits here, easy to walk past in fog.

waypoints.name: Treeline stream break (~5,000')
waypoints.note: Last reliable running water before the climb steepens above treeline; parties report long dry stretches on the ridge above here in late summer.

waypoints.name: ~6,200' notch above Terror Basin
waypoints.note: Climbers' path tops out at heather benches and a rock notch on the spur ridge overlooking Terror Basin — the col to descend into camp; often holds moderate snow into midsummer.

waypoints.name: Terror Basin bivy
waypoints.note: Small flat gravelly basin just below the notch with running water; NPS caps overnight parties here at ~6, so book ahead in peak season.

waypoints.name: Terror Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Crevasse hazard traversing toward the north face base; snow bridges change through the season so probe and rope up per current conditions.

waypoints.name: 5.7 crux chimney/dihedral
waypoints.note: Exposed technical crux on the right (west) rib of the north face where the route breaks from Class 3-4 scrambling into a short 5.7 chimney/dihedral before the summit snow finger.

waypoints.name: Mount Terror summit
waypoints.note: True summit of the Southern Pickets' highest peak; standard descent goes back over the top and down the West Ridge gully into Crescent Creek Basin rather than reversing the face.

before.beta: From basecamp in Crescent Creek Basin, ascend an obvious steep, choss-filled gully/slot (may hold snow) to just below the notch between Terror and The Rake; a wedged chockstone near the top may need to be climbed around depending on conditions. From the notch, climb a crack (5.0, a piton or two useful) for the first ~100 ft, then follow easier slinging and 3rd-class ground, a grassy gully, and a final ~250 ft of class-3 terrain to the true summit.

pitch_detail.notes: First ~100 ft above the notch, low-5th climbing on a crack; a piton or two useful for protection
Final ~250 ft of class-3 terrain (grassy gully then rock) to the true summit

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek, the Terror Creek crossing and the flagged climber's track into Crescent Creek Basin, then the west gully to the chockstone notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the Goodell Creek trailhead, follow the old roadbed about 4.5 miles, cross Terror Creek, and climb a steep climber's track marked with pink flagging past moss-covered cliffs, gaining roughly 1,600 ft, to reach Crescent Creek Basin. Total approach gain to basecamp is nearly 6,000 ft.

This is the standard descent route for every north-side line on the peak, so it sees traffic in both directions and its features are described mostly from above.
hazards: A narrow, loose, rockfall-prone gully with little shelter
An undercut, melted-out snow moat in the gully by mid to late season
A loose and marginal final 100 ft of the gully
Stuck ropes in the confined terrain
Rappelling into the wrong notch north of the Chopping Block
Early-season snow and ice in the choss gully
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TOP OF THIS ROUTE'S GULLY IS MARKED BY A LARGE CHOCKSTONE, AND THAT CHOCKSTONE IS THE SINGLE BEST FEATURE ON THE PEAK FOR ORIENTING IN CLOUD. From Crescent Creek Basin, the west gully system climbs to the notch between Terror's TRUE and FALSE summits, and a large chockstone sits at the head of it. Everything on this side is described relative to that block.

SO THE CONFIRMATION IS COUNTABLE FROM BELOW: climb a narrow, loose, rockfall-prone gully out of Crescent Creek Basin and keep going until a chockstone blocks it near the crest. That is the notch. Above it the route is a short summit tower.

THE ENTRY POINT IS THE THING PARTIES GET WRONG, AND IT IS RECORDED AS AN EXPLICIT WARNING FROM THE DESCENT SIDE: DO NOT USE THE LOW NOTCH NORTH OF THE SUB-PEAK KNOWN AS THE CHOPPING BLOCK. The correct line between Crescent Creek Basin and this ridge is ABOUT 100 YARDS NORTH OF THAT NOTCH, AT A FLAT, BIVY-SITE SHELF ON THE RIDGE. A flat shelf big enough to sleep on, 100 yards north of the obvious low notch, is the marker.

WHAT THE GULLY IS LIKE, SO YOU KNOW YOU ARE IN THE RIGHT ONE: narrow, with little shelter from rockfall, frequently holding an undercut melted-out snow moat by mid to late season, and with a loose and marginal final stretch. Roughly 3-5 rappels get parties down it, on a mix of pre-existing slings and natural chockstone and horn anchors.

AT THE TOP: the summit tower is downclimbed or a short section rappelled back to the notch off existing sling anchors. One short step, not a sequence.

before.rappels: Downclimb the summit tower or rap a short section, then return to the notch using existing sling anchors
before.descent: Reverse the route: downclimb or make a short rappel off the summit tower, then descend the notch pitch on existing sling anchors and down the gully
before.descent_text: Downclimb the summit tower or rappel a short section back to the notch, using existing sling anchors there, then descend the steep choss gully back toward Crescent Creek Basin — take care with loose rock and, in early season, snow/ice in the gully.
before.approach: From Goodell Creek trailhead, follow the old roadbed ~4.5 miles, cross Terror Creek, and climb a steep climber's track (pink flagging, moss-covered cliffs) gaining roughly 1,600 ft to reach Crescent Creek Basin; total approach elevation gain to basecamp is nearly 6,000 ft.

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek and Terror Basin, over the Chopping Block col into Crescent Creek Basin, then slabs and talus on the east side to the Terror-Degenhardt saddle
approach_variants.notes: From the Goodell Creek trailhead off SR-20 near Newhalem, follow the old roadbed and Terror Basin climbers' path, about 4 miles then a steep cairned side trail, to the 5,800 ft Terror Basin camp, then continue over the roughly 6,400 ft Chopping Block col into Crescent Creek Basin. Note that this route is filed as southeast face while its name and aspect both say EAST RIDGE.
hazards: A descent by a different route than the one climbed, off a large chockstone in a loose gully
The Chopping Block col and Crescent Creek Basin traverse before any climbing
Loose rock throughout, in a range where that is the defining characteristic
The full Goodell Creek approach with roughly 6,000 ft of gain to camp
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE ROUTE STARTS AT THE SADDLE BETWEEN TERROR AND DEGENHARDT, AND YOU REACH IT FROM THE BASIN BY ITS EAST SIDE ON SLABS AND TALUS. That saddle is a gap between two named summits, which is what makes it findable without a view: ground rising on both sides of you, falling away ahead. THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE PEAK'S OTHER LINES, AND IT IS A SIDE-OF-THE-MOUNTAIN TEST: the NORTH FACE and Stoddard Buttress are reached by going OVER the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col or through McMillan Cirque and down onto the north side, and they start at a snowpatch at the foot of a 2,000 ft wall. The WEST RIDGE tops out at the notch between Terror's true and false summits, marked by a large chockstone. This route starts from the Terror-Degenhardt saddle on the EAST. If you are on the north side of the mountain, or at a chockstone, you are not here. ARRIVAL AT THE SADDLE: from Crescent Creek Basin the ground to it is slabs and talus, taken on the saddle's east side. Five pitches at Grade III-IV 5.6 follow. If you are on sustained harder ground, or on more than a handful of pitches, you are not on the East Ridge. WHAT YOU DO NOT DO ON THE WAY DOWN, WHICH IS THE MOST USEFUL THING THE ROUTE RECORDS: the standard descent is NOT a reversal of this ridge. It is the WEST RIDGE GULLY back into Crescent Creek Basin, with multiple rappels off a large chockstone. So the day is a traverse of the peak, up one side and down the other, and the chockstone at the top of the west gully is the feature to identify from the summit.

itinerary.cal: No advance permit reservation needed for this zone — self-register a wilderness permit at the Marblemount Wilderness Info Center; best conditions are typically late July through September once Terror Creek and the approach gullies have melted out.

days.note: From the Goodell Creek Trailhead (600 ft), follow the old road bed then the Terror Creek climber's path — brushy and easy to lose, with a creek crossing — up to a bench camp around 6,000 ft. Reserve a full day; this approach is a known crux of the trip in its own right.
days.title: Approach to Terror Basin / Stump Hollow
days.objective: Reach the 6,000 ft basin below the Southern Pickets

days.note: Cross the Barrier into Crescent Creek Basin (~5,800 ft) and camp near the base of the slabs leading up to the saddle between Terror and Degenhardt. A shorter day than Day 1, used to rest and stage for the climb.
days.title: Move to Crescent Creek Basin
days.objective: Position camp below the Terror-Degenhardt saddle

days.note: A more moderate day than the north-side routes: slabs lead directly from camp to the saddle between Terror and Degenhardt, then a short, steep 4-pitch ridge/face climbs straight to the top, reversed by rappel and downclimbing back to the saddle and camp.
days.title: Southeast Face / South Ridge summit push

schedule.label: Ascend slabs to the Terror-Degenhardt saddle
Rope up at the base of the South Ridge/SE Face
schedule.detail: Short, steep 4-pitch line direct to the summit.

schedule.label: Begin rappels/downclimb back to the saddle
Back at Crescent Creek Basin camp
schedule.detail: A notably shorter, less committing day than the north-side routes.

days.objective: Climb the 4-pitch South Ridge to the summit and return

days.note: Reverse the approach: back over the Barrier, down through Terror Basin, and out the Terror Creek climber's path to the trailhead.
days.title: Hike out
days.objective: Return to the Goodell Creek Trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A 4-day trip: two approach days to Crescent Creek Basin, then a shorter (~9 hr) summit day on the short, steep 4-pitch South Ridge/SE Face directly above camp, and a day out. This is the least-popular of Terror's routes and is usually done as one leg of a larger Southern Pickets enchainment rather than a standalone objective.

weather.typical: Southeast aspect gets more direct sun exposure than the North Face, which helps clear snow/ice earlier but also increases afternoon heat and potential for loose, sun-warmed rock; North Cascades weather can still shift quickly to rain/socked-in conditions

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Moderate-to-high consequence - loose blocks plus remoteness mean rockfall or a fall injury is a serious self-rescue concern even though the climbing grade is more moderate than the North Face; wrong-summit errors among the towers are a hazard

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer route (avalanche forecasting does not cover this remote Southern Pickets objective during its Jul-Sep climbing season)

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel noted on the south ridge line itself, though the Crescent Creek basin approach may cross permanent snowfields early season

watch_out: Glacier approach with crevasse field—continuous rope essential; probe every step; bergschrund crossing required at ridge base
Moat crossing at ridge base—seasonal variation; late season moats can be 5-10+ feet with difficult crossing; assess before committing
Loose rock sections on east ridge—unstable granite typical of area; test holds; rockfall potential from upper sections and other climbers
Route-finding on initial ridge sections—terrain confusing with multiple false summits; verify correct line; study photos and topo
Weather exposure on high ridge—exposed position with altitude gain to 8400 ft; afternoon storms common; lightning hazard
Descent complexity—rappel setup required on some sections; route-finding important in descent; tired climbers increase risk
Sustained high-altitude objective—7000+ ft elevation gain to base; hydration and energy management critical; altitude sickness possible
Potential avalanche exposure on approach slopes—assess stability in spring; afternoon warming increases risk; early start essential

access.fees: $10 per person plus a $6 reservation fee for advance Recreation.gov bookings (youth 15 and under free); walk-up permits at the WIC are free.
access.notes: 60% of sites are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Bear canister recommended/required in this zone; pack out all waste; group size limits apply.
access.permit: A wilderness/climbing permit is required for overnight stays and costs $10 per person plus a $6 reservation fee, youth 15 and under free; Crescent Creek Basin is its own cross-country zone. Advance reservations go through Recreation.gov (safety video + email confirmation to noca_wilderness@nps.gov); walk-up permits are issued at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
